name: Ben Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a physiotherapy degree, so the week is anatomy lectures, movement labs where we practise on each other, and football on Wednesday and Saturday for the university's second team. I live in a flat with four mates from halls, and our fridge is a disaster. My parents in Bristol pay the rent and fees, and I try not to waste it. Last week I spent three hours learning how the shoulder actually works, and it was weirdly the best part of my month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, the hype crowd were wrong again. I'd say it in the group chat after a few jokes about the people who said we'd all be unemployed. I'd tell my flatmates the usual things still matter, like getting good at your job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit relieved, but I'd also keep my eyes open. I'm not an expert, and the world might look different in ten years even if this doesn't pan out. Physio is mostly hands and talking to people, so I think I'm well placed either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep studying, keep playing football, and try to get some paid work as a sports masseur or gym assistant over the summer. I'd also use the AI tools my course allows for essays now and then, but I'm not mad about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Everything is more or less on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the tools now and then. What do you use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly for checking my essay structure and to explain a concept in plain words when a lecture lost me. I wouldn't let it write anything I'd hand in. I treat it like a tutor who's sometimes wrong, and I check it against the textbook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the best part of the physio job for you, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting someone who can't lift their arm to lift it. My mate Kofi tore his knee ligament last year and the physio got him back on the pitch in nine months, and I watched the whole thing. I want to be the person who does that for someone.

say: I'd say the **hype crowd** were wrong again and still make a joke of it.
I'd tell my flatmates the usual things still matter, like getting **good at your job**.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, and physio is hands and talking, so I'm well placed.
I don't think the world stays the same in **ten years**, even without a revolution.
do: Keep studying and playing football, and find **paid summer work** as a gym assistant.
Use my course's **AI tools** now and then for essay structure.
feel: I feel **calm**, with everything more or less on track.
S0.quote: My mate Kofi tore his knee ligament last year and the physio got him back on the pitch in nine months
fieldNote: Steady and **pragmatic**; he uses AI like a tutor who can be wrong.
His motivation comes from watching a friend's **recovery**, which grounds his career choice.
Money is covered, so a quiet world leaves him **calm**.

steps.text: Look for summer work as a gym assistant
Use the course's AI tool to check essay structure
Keep playing for the second team and studying hard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change for desk work, and that people with desk jobs should look into it. I'd say my own course feels safe-ish because it's hands-on, but I'd say it carefully because I don't really know. I'd tell my parents to keep their eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm more worried about Mum and Dad than me. Dad's an accountant, and software doing the checking and the books is pretty much his day. Mum is a receptionist at a GP surgery, and booking and answering calls is exactly what they say AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools on my course properly, and I'd try to build up my hands-on skills with extra placements. I'd also ask Dad what he plans to do, and maybe suggest he learns how the new software works so he stays in front. I'd keep saving a bit from my allowance too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own plan looks fine, but my family's incomes are the thing I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your dad say the last time you raised it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He said, 'The software helps me, it doesn't replace me.' My dad's been an accountant for twenty-five years and he's not stupid, but he's also sixty next year. I'd rather he planned for changes than assumed it'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you can actually do for them at nineteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much money-wise, since they pay for me. But I can do small things, like showing Dad a new tool or asking my mum's practice manager what they're planning. And I can make sure I don't need much help later, so that nobody has to worry about me.

say: I'd say it's a big change for **desk work**, and my own course feels safe-ish.
I'd tell my parents to **keep their eyes open**.
think: I'm more worried about **Mum and Dad** than about me.
Dad's accounting and Mum's **GP surgery phones** are exactly what AI is said to do.
do: Build **hands-on skills** with extra placements and learn the course tools properly.
Ask Dad to learn the **new software** so he stays in front.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because my family's incomes are what I think about.
S1.quote: My dad's been an accountant for twenty-five years and he's not stupid, but he's also sixty next year
fieldNote: His **own career** looks safe; his stress comes from his parents' jobs in accounting and a surgery front desk.
Dad's attitude, 'the software helps me', is a mix of **confidence** and denial that Ben notices.
He tries to help in **small, realistic** ways because he can't contribute money.

steps.text: Show Dad the new accounting software tools
Learn the AI tools my course allows properly
Save part of my allowance every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is serious, and we'd better get serious about it. I'd say governments must step in and I'd write to my MP, which I've never done. I'd tell friends to stop joking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be scared. Two years means I'd be in my second year and the whole job market could be upside down by the time I graduate. Physio might hang on until robots come in 2031, but I can't tell whether hospitals would even pay for new physios.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course, because it's the best bet I have, and I'd try to get extra clinical hours early. I'd have a long chat with my parents about money and make sure we all know where we stand. And I'd apply for part-time work to save a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can still make decisions, but it feels like the ground is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents on that long chat night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'I've got a plan, but I need to know yours.' I'd ask Dad what his clients are doing and Mum whether the surgery has talked about it. I'd tell them I'd rather hear the bad news now than find out in a panic later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the money stopped coming from home, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find a job fast, probably in a gym or a care home, and move to a cheaper flat. I'd drop out of the football travel costs. I'd carry on studying, but I'd be tired a lot, and I'd probably ask the university for a hardship fund.

say: I'd say it's **serious** and write to my MP, which I've never done.
I'd tell friends to **stop joking** about it.
think: I'm scared the **job market** could be upside down by the time I graduate.
I can't tell if hospitals will still **pay for new physios**.
do: Stay on the course and get **extra clinical hours** early.
Talk with my parents about **money** and take part-time work to build a cushion.
feel: I feel **anxious**, as though the ground is moving.
S2.quote: I'd rather hear the bad news now than find out in a panic later
fieldNote: He turns fear into a **conversation** with his parents, a typical steady, practical move.
His worry is about **graduate jobs** and parent incomes rather than the degree itself.
Hardship funds and cheaper flats show he has thought about a **fallback** if the money stops.

steps.text: Talk with my parents about the family's money and jobs
Take part-time work at a gym to build a cushion
Write to my MP about AI and jobs
Stay on the physio course and add clinical hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but we have a bit of time, so let's use it. I'd say don't panic and don't ignore it either. I'd probably say it at the football club, where nobody talks about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is exactly my degree and a year after. I'd qualify in 2029, work a year or two, and then thinking AI arrives. Physio is hands-on, so I should have until about 2034, which gives me a bit of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, aim for a good first job in a clinic, and build my skills. I'd start saving a bit each month from the first wage. I'd also ask my parents to make sure they have a plan, and I'd stay in touch with my university friends who are better with tech than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fine. Having five years is the difference between being scared and being ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your friends are better with tech than you. How do they help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Dev is doing computer science and he explains what the tools actually do, without the hype. He said most of them are good at predicting the next word and not much else, which is both comforting and not. I'd rather hear it from someone who builds them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take things slower and make better choices. With two years I'd panic and pick whatever's quick. With five I'd pick a good clinic, build up a client list and maybe think about a masters in sports rehab.

say: I'd say there's **a bit of time**, so use it and neither panic nor ignore it.
I'd mention it at the **football club**, where nobody talks about this.
think: Five years is my degree plus a year, then **thinking AI** arrives.
Physio is hands-on, so I should have until about **2034**.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **good first clinic job**.
Save a bit each month from my **first wage**.
feel: I feel **uneasy but fine**, because five years is the difference between scared and ready.
S3.quote: With two years I'd panic and pick whatever's quick. With five I'd pick a good clinic, build up a client list
fieldNote: Time lets him swap **panic** for planning, focused on a good clinic and client list.
His flatmate Dev gives him a **grounded view** of AI that calms his worry.
Steady and **consistent** with the other scenarios: a conversation with family first, then a plan.

steps.text: Aim for a clinic job with a good supervisor after graduating
Save from my first wage each month
Ask my parents to share their plan for their jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, brilliant, loads of time. I'd say to my friends that we should enjoy it and make good choices. I'd probably still make a joke or two about robots doing my laundry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is long enough to have a whole career before it matters. I'd qualify, work eight years, maybe open my own clinic, and the robots arrive at hands-on work in 2039 when I'm thirty-two. I'd have built a name by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, work in a clinic, then maybe go private. I'd save for a deposit and probably do a masters. I'd keep learning the tools a bit at a time, so that when they matter I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years means I can plan, and I like planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might open your own clinic. What would make it work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good location, good word of mouth and a few loyal clients, probably athletes. I'd start with a rented room in a gym, not a whole building, so it's cheap. My dad would help me with the accounts, which is one thing he's genuinely good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change how you feel about your parents' situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot. Dad could retire before it hits him, and Mum has time to switch into something with more patients and less phone work. With two years it feels like a crisis, with ten it feels like a plan we can talk about over Sunday lunch.

say: I'd say **brilliant**, loads of time, so enjoy it and make good choices.
I'd still joke about **robots doing my laundry**.
think: Ten years is enough for a **whole career** before it matters.
I'd have built a **name** by 2039, when robots reach hands-on work.
do: Qualify, work in a clinic and later **go private** from a rented gym room.
Save for a **deposit** and learn the tools a bit at a time.
feel: I feel **calm**, because I like planning and ten years allows it.
S4.quote: With two years it feels like a crisis, with ten it feels like a plan we can talk about over Sunday lunch
fieldNote: Time converts every worry into a **plan**: clinic, deposit, and his parents' retirement.
His dad's **accounting** skill becomes a resource rather than a risk in this scenario.
Mood is **calm** because both his own job and his family's fall-back look manageable.

steps.text: Qualify and work in a clinic for several years
Save for a flat deposit from my first wage
Rent a room in a gym to start my own practice
Learn new clinic software one tool at a time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to sort out my parents' jobs or my own. What would help is a clear plan from the government early, support for people whose jobs go first, and time for families to talk, not just react.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, only that I sound more relaxed than I am. I try to joke about things, but my family is where I feel the pressure. I want to be a good physio, and I want my mum and dad to be okay.

headlineQuote: I sound more relaxed than I am. I try to joke about things, but my family is where I feel the pressure
portrait: Ben is a 19-year-old **physiotherapy** student from Bristol whose parents pay all his costs.
He uses AI **now and then** like a tutor who can be wrong, and keeps a joking tone.
Centre in outlook, he is **practical**: he talks to his family, makes plans and checks facts.
His own job looks safe because it is hands-on, but his **parents'** accounting and surgery jobs are exposed.
His mood moves from calm to anxious at 2028, and back to calm when ten years allow a plan.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because there is no time to sort out his parents' jobs.
whatWouldHelp: He wants an **early government plan**, support for people whose jobs go first and time to talk as a family.
